newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia seen relying on corn imports this year.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia seen relying on corn imports this year.

text.p: Indonesia's corn imports are expected to rise marginally this year despite the launch of an ambitious programme to boost domestic production, an industry official said on Wednesday.
Budiarto Soebijanto, chairman of the Federation of Feedmeal Producers, however, said imports would fall significantly next year if the planting programme was successful.
Corn is an important ingredient in animal feeds. It is also consumed by humans in the form of oil and processed products.
"Corn imports this year are expected to be about one million tonnes, compared with 800,000-900,000 tonnes last year," Soebijanto told Reuters in an interview.
He said 500,000 tonnes of corn had already been imported so far this year, and that a similar quantity was expected to be imported in the second half of 1997.
"The actual numbers would depend on the local corn harvest in the second semester of this year," he said.
The corn harvest in East Java, which totals about 30 percent of the annual national production, was expected to get underway next month and last through September.
Traders said feedmills and the trading community would closely monitor the harvest before deciding on how much they would need to import this year.
"The exact import numbers would depend on the size of the harvest," one senior trader said. "So far, there have been no indications to show that the crop would not be normal in size."

The traders also said the success of the government's push to cultivate a high-yielding hybrid corn variety had been overstated, adding that imports were expected to continue in 1998 although the volume might be smaller.
Agriculture Minister Syarifuddin Baharsyah said early this month that Indonesia's corn production was expected to increase to 10.5 million tonnes this year from 9.1 million tonnes in 1996.
Soebijanto said although there had been some progress in the hybrid-corn planting programme it had not been satisfactory.
"The government has set a target of planting 500,000 hectares with hybrid corn this year, which could raise production by an additional 1.5 million tonnes," he said.
"There will be a significant decline in imports next year if domestic corn production increased," he added. "We don't need to import if 500,000 hectares are planted (with hybrid corn)."
On the government's proposal to slap an import duty on corn, Soebijanto said the move, if implemented, could see the fast-growing poultry industry facing higher production costs.
"Poultry farmers will see higher production costs and will be not keen on expanding their business while meat consumption continues to increase due to rising incomes.
"A decline in poultry production will mean less demand for corn, which will affect corn farmers," he said.

Syarifuddin said the government was studying whether to impose an import duty on corn or find other ways to boost domestic corn prices. The import duty on corn was scrapped under an economic deregulation package in 1995.
